meta.title: Tajik (забони тоҷикӣ) Language Ontology
meta.description: Description of Modern Literary Tajik, an Eastern variety of New Persian used in Tajikistan and parts of Uzbekistan. The variety described is the literary standard in Cyrillic.
sources: Gernot Windfuhr and John R. Perry, Persian and Tajik (chapter 8 of The Iranian Languages), attached chapter, printed page numbers 416-544. Descriptive reference grammar. URL not stated in the attached file. License not stated in the attached file.

Nasrullo Khojayori and Mikael Thompson, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners, 2009, Georgetown University Press, ISBN 978-1-58901-269-1. Pedagogical reference grammar. URL not stated in the attached file. Copyright 2009 Georgetown University Press, as printed in the attached file.
meta.classification: Eastern variety of New Persian; Iranian. Evolved from Early New Persian. Western Persian (Iran) and Eastern Persian (Afghanistan and Central Asia) are the two broad groups; Tajik belongs to the Eastern group.
meta.location: Tajikistan and parts of Uzbekistan, including the cities of Bukhara and Samarkand; also Tajik Persian speakers in Afghanistan and a minority in Kirgizstan. The so-called Tajiks of south-west Xinjiang speak Pamir languages, not Persian.
meta.standard_dialect: Modern Literary Tajik (zabon-i adabi-i hozira-i tojik), planned in the Soviet period and based loosely on the style of Bukhara. Dushanbe is nominally in the Northern dialect area but is best considered separately.
meta.scope: Standard literary Tajik of the modern written norm associated with Dushanbe, in Cyrillic script, as described for Modern Literary Tajik.
meta.note: Speaker figure, location, dialect groups, and the literary standard are synchronous descriptions in Windfuhr & Perry (book pp. 420-421). The Eastern vs Western split and descent from Early New Persian are diachronic as well as synchronic (book pp. 416-421). ISO codes are file identity fields; the attached grammars do not print ISO 639 codes.

gaps.fact: Three distinct buffer vowels -а-, -я-, and -й- each with three examples, as separate morphological formatives
gaps.reason: The sources attest euphonic -y- after vowels, ezafe -yi, and euphonic -g- after -a. They do not set up three vowel buffers under those names.

gaps.fact: Homonymy of possessive -ат, -аш, -амон, -атон, -ашон with verbal personal endings of the same shape
gaps.reason: The Tajik verb endings in the paradigm are -am, -i, -ad, -em, -ed, -and. Only -am clearly matches an enclitic of the same shape. -at/-as/-amon/-aton/-ason are enclitics.

Language.definition: A complex sign system organized as a lexicon and a grammar. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Language] Applied here to Modern Literary Tajik (synchrony): a variety of New Persian, zabon-i tojiki / zabon-i forsi-i tojik, fostered since the 1920s as the national and literary language of Tajikistan.
key_properties: Eastern New Persian (synchrony), evolved from Early New Persian (diachrony)
Cyrillic orthography since 1939/1940, after Arabic and a Latin stage (diachrony of the writing system; the modern orthography is synchronous)
Six-vowel system and retention of the q vs gh contrast, unlike Iranian Persian (synchrony)
Language.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 416-421, 425

Linguistic_System.definition: The grammar and lexicon of a language variety. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticSystem] For this file, the system is Modern Literary Tajik unless a dialect is named.
Linguistic_System.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

Linguistic_Taxon.definition: A node in a classification of languages. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticTaxon]

taxonomy.genetic: New Persian, Eastern group (Afghanistan and Central Asia), as opposed to the Western group mainly in Iran
taxonomy.geographic: Tajikistan; Bukhara and Samarkand in Uzbekistan; continuum with Afghan Persian interrupted by Turkmen and Uzbek
taxonomy.political: National and literary language of Tajikistan (Soviet republic, independent state from 1991)
taxonomy.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 417-421

Genetic_Taxon.definition: A taxon based on inheritance. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GeneticTaxon] Tajik and Iranian Persian both evolved from Early New Persian (diachrony). Tajik has retained Early Eastern Persian features and has assimilated a Turkic typological component (diachrony); both still share much of the underlying system (synchrony).
Genetic_Taxon.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 416-420

Geographic_Taxon.definition: A taxon based on place. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GeographicTaxon] Four dialect groups follow the Oxus basin: Northern lowlands (Bukhara, Samarkand, Derbend, Ferghana Valley including Khujand, down the Varzob valley toward Dushanbe); Central (upper Zarafshon); Southern (Kulob, Qarotegin including Gharm, toward the Pamirs); South-eastern (Darvoz, on the bend of the Oxus near Rushan).
Geographic_Taxon.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

Political_Taxon.definition: A taxon based on a polity. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PoliticalTaxon] Tajik has been fostered as the national literary language of Tajikistan since the 1920s (synchrony of status; the political history is diachrony).
Political_Taxon.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 420

Endangerment_Taxon.definition: A taxon based on degree of endangerment. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/EndangermentTaxon] The attached sources do not assign an endangerment status to Standard Tajik. They do note assimilation and emigration for Caucasian Tat, and emigration of the Jews of Bukhara, which is a Northern Tajik sub-variety, not the national standard.
Endangerment_Taxon.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 418, 421

Language_Family.definition: A genetic grouping. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LanguageFamily] The attached chapter treats Tajik inside Iranian, as New Persian. A finer Indo-European subtree is not stated in the attached sources.
Language_Family.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 416-417

Language_Subfamily.definition: A grouping inside a family. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LanguageSubfamily] Persian varieties split into a Western group (mainly Iran) and an Eastern group (Afghanistan and Central Asia). Tajik is Eastern (synchrony of the split; the split itself is diachronic).
Language_Subfamily.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 417

Dialect.definition: A regional or social variety differing from the standard. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Dialect]

list.name: Northern
list.note: Bukhara, Samarkand, Derbend, Ferghana Valley including Khujand, and the Varzob valley toward Dushanbe. Influenced by Uzbek, with widespread bilingualism (synchrony). A sub-variety is the speech of the Jews of Bukhara. In Northern dialects an -ro construction widely replaces the ezafe: man-a pisar-am 'my son' (synchrony, dialectal).
list.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 421, 443

list.name: Central
list.note: Upper Zarafshon (Zeravshan) valley. The attached chapter names the group and does not list phonetic or morphological differences peculiar to it.
list.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

list.name: Southern
list.note: South and east of the capital, Kulob and Qarotegin (Karategin), including Gharm, as far as the Pamirs. Affinities with left-bank Badakhshan in Afghanistan. Tendency to drop h in all positions, and to drop r before d in a few common words, especially the past stem of kardan (kad-um 'I did') (synchrony, dialectal).
list.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 421, 429

list.name: South-eastern
list.note: Darvoz, on the bend of the Oxus near Rushan. Affinities with Badakhshan. Includes Tajik as the contact vernacular (called forsi) of Gorno-Badakhshan.
list.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

list.name: Dushanbe
list.note: Nominally Northern, but a small market town made capital in 1924, with later demographic change. Best considered separately from the Northern dialects. The literary variety described in the chapter is Modern Literary Tajik, not a transcript of Dushanbe speech.
list.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

The_Linguistic_Sign.definition: A pairing of form and meaning. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticSign] Tajik orthographic words in Cyrillic are the written signs of the literary language (synchrony).
The_Linguistic_Sign.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 423-425; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners

Linguistic_Unit.definition: A unit of linguistic structure. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticUnit] Units used below include the phoneme, the syllable, the morpheme (stem, affix, clitic), the word, and the clause.
Linguistic_Unit.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8

Literary_Language.definition: Modern Literary Tajik, zabon-i adabi-i hozira-i tojik (synchrony).
Literary_Language.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 421

Language_varieties.standard_vs_dialect: Examples in Windfuhr & Perry are Modern Literary Tajik unless a dialect is named. Khojayori & Thompson describe Tajiki, and mark some forms as literary/formal versus colloquial northern or southern.
Language_varieties.Bukharan_note: Windfuhr & Perry identify Bukharan Jewish speech as a Northern sub-variety with a modest literature. Most speakers of that variety have emigrated.

Phonetics_and_Phonology.note: Vowel count and the q/gh contrast are synchronous facts of Modern Standard Tajik. Length neutralization relative to Early New Persian is diachrony. Orthography is synchronous for the current Cyrillic norm.

phonemes.quality: low; unstable; more open than Russian a, without a w-glide
phonemes.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 425-426; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners, alphabet chapter

phonemes.quality: mid front; stable. Word-initially e is written with non-yotated э; after a consonant the letter е can represent simple e
phonemes.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 423, 425-426; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners

phonemes.quality: high front; unstable. Lowered to e before h or glottal stop plus a consonant
phonemes.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 426
Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 425-426; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners

phonemes.quality: high back; unstable. Lowered to uu before h or glottal stop plus a consonant
phonemes.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 426

phonemes.quality: high back rounded; stable; more close than u, and slightly lower
phonemes.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 426; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners lists у and ӯ as distinct vowels

Vowel_inventory.stable_vs_unstable: Stable (phonetically invariant): e, uu, o. Unstable (length and quality vary): i, a, u. In stressed position and in unstressed closed syllables the unstable vowels match the stable vowels in length; in unstressed open syllables they may shorten or drop. Examples: did '(s)he saw', d'gar 'other'; dud 'smoke', g'doz 'melting'; bad 'bad', b'dan 'body'. Synchrony. In some dialects, for example Bukhara, phonemic length is preserved in i and u.
Vowel_inventory.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 425-426
Vowel_inventory.diachrony: Both Modern Standard Persian and Tajik reduced the eight-vowel inventory of Middle and Early New Persian to six, in different ways. In some varieties of Tajik, length was neutralized by merger of short and long high vowels and rounding of long aa (diachrony).

Consonant_inventory.count_statement: Windfuhr & Perry: 30 Tajik segmental phonemes against 29 in Persian. The single consonantal difference is that Early New Persian gh (velar fricative) and loaned uvular q merged in Persian and did not merge in Tajik (diachrony of the merger; the contrast is synchronous in Tajik). Khojayori & Thompson: the Cyrillic alphabet has 24 consonant letters.
contrasts_named_in_prose: v varies with w: bilabial w finally, between rounded vowels, and after a before a consonant (varaq 'page', beva 'widow', but gov 'cow', suwol 'question', qawl 'speech')
palatal fricative of limited distribution; in spoken Tajik, including Russian loans, it tends to be replaced by j
glottal stop from an automatic onset, from Arabic hamza, and from Arabic ayn
k and g are fronted before front vowels under Uzbek influence
Consonant_inventory.letters_note: The 24 consonant letters are those read from the alphabet list in Khojayori & Thompson. Windfuhr & Perry describe the same system in transliteration (stops and affricates p b t d ch j k g q; fricatives f s z sh zh x gh h; nasals m n; liquid l and trill r; glides y and v/w) and state the 30-phoneme total rather than a letter count.
Consonant_inventory.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 423-427; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners, chapter 1

Stress.nominals: Word-final in nominals, including nominal verb forms (synchrony). Examples: baca 'child', did-an 'to see'. Trisyllabics have secondary initial stress: baca-g-i 'childhood'.
Stress.finite_verbs: Stress in verb forms is regressive, less so in Tajik than in Persian. me- and na- are stressed, and na- takes primary stress: na-me-rav-am 'I will not go'. With bi-, Tajik has primary stress on the final syllable and secondary stress on the prefix: bi-gir-ed. Unprefixed past forms may stress either the stem or the personal ending: guft-em or guft-em. The definite-future pattern keeps stress on the personal ending: xah-am raft 'I will go'.
Stress.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 429-430; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners states that stress usually falls on the first syllable in finite verb forms or on the last syllable in nouns and noun-like words

Orthography.statement: Khojayori & Thompson: a modified Cyrillic alphabet became official in 1940 and contains 35 letters: 24 consonants, 6 vowels plus и with macron (ӣ) used at the end of a word, and 4 yotated letters (е, ё, ю, я). Windfuhr & Perry: Arabic script was replaced by Latin in 1928 and by Cyrillic in 1939; six supplementary letters are added to the Cyrillic inventory by diacritics (diachrony of script change; the inventory is synchronous).
Orthography.dotted_i: ӣ (macron) marks stressed word-final -i of a morphological formative, as against unstressed ezafe -i. The macron is dropped before an ezafe. Also used in monosyllables: ki 'who?' (distinct from unstressed subordinizer ki), chi 'what?', si 'thirty', and the interrogative enclitic -mi.
Orthography.distinct_letters: Tajik keeps ҳ, қ, ғ, ҷ as letters. Windfuhr & Perry: қ (q) is distinct from the velar stop, and ғ (gh) is distinct from х, unlike the Persian merger of q and gh. Khojayori lists ҳ, қ, ғ, ҷ among the consonant letters, separate from х, к, г, ч.
Orthography.yotated_letters: е, ё, ю, я represent y plus a vowel. Russian-style и after a vowel represents yi, as in the ezafe after a vowel (xona-yi man 'my house').
Orthography.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book pp. 420, 423-424; Khojayori & Thompson 2009, Tajiki Reference Grammar for Beginners, chapter 1

Buffer_vowels.statement: No two adjacent vowels are allowed in standard Persian and Tajik (synchrony). Hiatus breakers attested for Tajik are -y- and, with the copula and with indefinite and derivational -i, a glottal stop. Windfuhr & Perry also call -y- a euphonic consonant interposed after vowels before pronominal enclitics. Khojayori & Thompson describe -гӣ (not a bare vowel) as the form of the abstract suffix after the vowel а.

y_after_vowel_before_enclitic_or_ending.fact: A euphonic -y- stands between a vowel and a following pronominal enclitic or personal ending (synchrony).

g_before_stressed_suffix_after_a.fact: Word-final -a alternates with -ag- before stressed -on, -ona, and -i. In Tajik this g is treated as euphonic and is supplied even for non-Persian words in -a (synchrony). Diachronically -ag continues Middle Persian -ag.

Syllable.structure: CV, CVC, CVCC. Examples: to 'till', dar 'in', dast 'hand'. Syllable boundary is any consonant before a vowel: dast-am [das-tam] 'my hand'.

number.statement: Singular is unmarked. Plurals are -ho and -on (synchrony). -ho applies to all nouns. -on is more limited, stylistically literary, and relatively more frequent in Tajik than in Persian.

two_stems.fact: Every verb has Stem I (present stem) and Stem II (past stem). Past tenses, the past participle, and the infinitive are built on Stem II. Present tenses are built on Stem I (synchrony). Stem II ends in a dental, -d or -t.
two_stems.regular: In the regular class, Stem II is Stem I plus -id. Example: ras- / rasid- 'arrive'.

borrowing.arabic: Approximately 50 percent of the Persian/Tajik lexicon, about 25 percent in frequency of use (Windfuhr & Perry, for the Persian phonology section, applied to the shared loan component). Broken plurals and the adverbial suffix -an are morphological residues (diachrony), still present as vocabulary (synchrony).
borrowing.turkic_uzbek: Uzbek bilingualism in Northern dialects. Loan morphology includes a kim- series of indefinites (kim-ki 'someone or other, anyone', kim-kadom 'some N or other') and kinship terms such as aka, uka, yanga. Postpositions such as -dan are dialect borrowings, not Modern Literary Tajik.
borrowing.russian: Systematic introduction of Russian loans in the Soviet period (diachrony). Initial clusters foreign to Tajik occur in loans (zveno 'team', Stalinobod, the former name of Dushanbe) and may be assimilated by speakers to varying degrees (synchrony). istansa from Russian stantsiya. Address: rafiq 'comrade', patronymics, surnames in -ov/-ova.

suffix.definition: An affix that follows the host. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/suffix]

prefix.definition: An affix that precedes the host. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/prefix]

allomorph.definition: An alternate shape of a morpheme. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/allomorph]

geneticallyRelated.instantiated_by: Modern Literary Tajik is genetically related to Iranian Persian: both evolved from Early New Persian.

agrees.definition: Shares grammatical features with another constituent. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/agrees]
agrees.instantiated_by: The finite verb agrees with the subject in person and number (me-rav-am vs me-rav-and). Adjectives do not agree in number (Khojayori & Thompson).

orthographicRep.definition: Written form. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/orthographicRep] Cyrillic for forms taken from Khojayori & Thompson; Latin transliteration for forms taken from Windfuhr & Perry, who state that Modern Literary Tajik examples are transliterated.
orthographicRep.source: Windfuhr & Perry, Persian and Tajik, in The Iranian Languages, ch. 8, book p. 423

stringRep.definition: A literal string of a form. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/stringRep] The form fields in this file are string representations.
